job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Esther Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake up at eight, make tea, and cycle to Tidewell, a thirty-person startup in Bristol that makes booking software for village halls and community venues. I'm the only junior in a team of six developers, so I mostly fix small bugs, write tests and build simple pages with an AI assistant open beside me all day. I did a software degree and scraped a pass, with no internship, but I built projects at night and that's what got me hired. Evenings are my tenants' union meeting or my side project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, but kindly. I use AI every day for boilerplate and tests, and it's a good assistant, not a replacement. At work I'd say let's keep shipping. Online I'd probably post a thread about hype cycles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd be pleased, because Tidewell keeps its junior roles. If AI stays a good assistant and nothing more, I keep my junior job and only have to worry about rent. And rent is plenty on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building and use the tools to ship faster, and ask for a small raise at my six-month review. I'd put 150 pounds a month into savings and start a rota app for the tenants' union as a side project. I'd keep going to the tenants' meetings too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Relaxed, mostly. A bit of me is bored, because I like the big-change stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you only worry about rent. What's the rent situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our landlord put the rent up 8 percent in spring, and my housemates Nia and Sam and I talk about leaving every month. We're writing letters through the tenants' union, but a letter isn't a fix. If I lost hours at Tidewell I'd be out of the room in a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who's still looking for a first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the market is slow, not dead, and a small project on GitHub beats a hundred cover letters. My friend Dara got her job in a bank's IT team by fixing a bug in an open-source library. I'd offer to read her application.

Online I'd post a thread about **hype cycles**.
think: I'd be pleased because Tidewell keeps its **junior roles**.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the union fight starts. If AI writes the code, firms should pay into retraining and nobody should be sacked for using it well. At work I'd say let's show what we can do with it, so we set the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the junior, and what AI replaces fastest is junior work: small bug fixes, tests, simple pages. My boss Priya might think one senior with AI equals one senior plus a junior. I'm adaptive, but I can't out-code the tool on easy stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the parts the tool is bad at: talking to customers, working out what a hall manager really needs, and checking the AI's work. I'd ask Priya to put me on customer calls. I'd save 250 pounds a month and keep the side project as a Plan B. I'd push the tenants' union and a tech workers' union to join forces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a buzz. It feels like standing at the edge of a pool: scary and a little thrilling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the part of your job you think AI is bad at?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing what the customer means. A hall manager says it should just work like our paper diary, and you have to understand what that means in their head. A tool will build exactly what you ask, even if that's the wrong thing, and I'm the one who has to know what the customer means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about the other juniors you know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friends who learned to code at a bootcamp and don't use these tools. They're doing what I did two years ago, and the market for that is shrinking. I'd tell them to start using it today, even if it feels like cheating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need emergency politics: a basic income, a four-day week, public ownership of the biggest models. I'd say it online loudly. At work I'd say let's make Tidewell the firm that does this well, because that's how we keep jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is gone in two years, or turned into something I can't recognise. A pass degree, no internship, and I'm competing with a thing that writes code in seconds. I'm not alone in that, but it isn't comforting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself useful to Priya in ways AI can't yet: customer calls and testing on real devices at venues. I'd save 400 pounds a month, move to a cheaper room, and join the tech union drive. If it all went wrong I'd go to my mum's in Swindon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry. I worked hard to get into this field, and it feels like the door is closing as I step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the anger go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the people building it and selling it as inevitable. The tool isn't at fault, the owners are, and I'd want them taxed, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do on the first day your job disappeared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Call my mum, then text Nia and Sam, then update my CV before breakfast, then go to the tenants' union office, because I'd need a roomful of people who'd get it. I'd hate being alone with it.

say: I'd say we need **emergency politics**: basic income, a four-day week and public ownership.
At work I'd say let's make Tidewell the firm that does it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do it right, so let's. A retraining guarantee, a shorter week, and tech workers organised. At work I'd keep trying new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm a little hopeful. In five years I'll be 27, with experience, which is when it matters. I think entry-level coding jobs will mostly vanish, but I'd have already moved to the part that's about customers and design.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 250 pounds a month, build the side project into something real, and take a part-time course in product design. I'd also ask Priya to rotate me into customer work next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but motivated. It feels like a race I can actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Race against whom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Other juniors and the tools, honestly. I'd want to be on the right side of it in three years, when the juniors who didn't start now are competing for the last few posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum, who's a teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That teaching is probably safer than coding, which she'd find funny. I'd tell her I'm not scared, just busy, and she'd say I should take time off. Five years goes quicker than you'd think, so I can't take time off from learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a decade to rebuild the whole deal: education, tax and the working week. At work I'd say let's not wait for the last two years. I'd say it to the tenants' union too, because housing is part of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be pretty fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, and I'd either have my own small company or be in a role with customers that AI can't do. I might even like the world better, if the gains get shared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, save 200 pounds a month, and start the part-time design course. I'd think about buying a place with Nia, though prices might fall, so I'd wait. I'd also vote and canvass for whoever backs a short working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some hope. It's the only picture where I see a long life and not a scramble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably start the company. A tiny firm building booking tools for community halls, with the AI doing most of the code and me doing the talking. It'd be me and one friend, not twenty people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a decade make you less urgent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, which is a risk. Ten years can feel like forever until it's two years, so I'd set myself a yearly check on what I can do that the tool can't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my whole job sits right in the path. I'm junior, I code, and I'm competing with something that writes code in seconds. What would help is real politics: a basic income, retraining that's paid for, and a proper say for workers over how these tools come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not scared of the tool, I use it every day. I'm scared of who owns it and what they do with the gains. Anything that helps us share it, like unions and tax, would help more than another course.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the tool, I use it every day. I'm scared of who owns it and what they do with the gains.
portrait: **Esther**, 22, is the only junior developer at a Bristol startup, with a pass degree and no internship but strong **side projects**.
She uses AI every day and is the most adaptive of the group, yet her job is the one **most exposed**.
Progressive and active in a tenants' union, she blames **owners** and wants tax, unions and a shorter week.
Her mood peaks at **alarmed** at two years and returns to calm at ten, with a tiny firm of her own.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, where the junior coding job she just won may vanish in two years.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and paid retraining, plus a say for workers over how tools arrive.
Taxes that make the **owners** share the gains.
